Core Rendering

49→

Edge Rasterization, Shape Drawing, and Blend Modes

50→
51→ 52→
53→

Introduction

55→

56→ Core rendering forms the foundation of the entire graphics engine. Every shape drawn on screen—whether a simple rectangle or a complex curved path—ultimately becomes a collection of edges that are rasterized into pixels through a scanline algorithm. 57→

58→

59→ This section establishes the fundamental building blocks: drawing rectangles, implementing edge-based rasterization, and creating a full Porter-Duff alpha blending system. It then extends this foundation to handle arbitrary convex polygons with viewport clipping, enabling the rendering of triangles, pentagons, and any other convex shape. 60→

61→

62→ This page covers the core algorithms that make it all work: how shapes are converted to edges, how those edges are walked scanline-by-scanline, how alpha values are properly composited, and how shapes are clipped to stay within the viewport boundaries. 63→

64→
65→ 66→
67→
68→ 71→ 74→ 77→ 80→
81→ 82→
83→ 84→
85→

Edge-Based Rendering

86→

87→ The graphics engine uses an edge-based scanline algorithm for all shape rendering. Every shape—rectangle, triangle, polygon, path—is first converted into a list of edges. Each edge represents one side of the shape, storing the top and bottom Y coordinates, the X position, and the slope (how X changes as Y increments). 88→

89→

90→ The scanline algorithm then processes the frame buffer row by row. For each Y coordinate, it finds all active edges, calculates their X intersections, and fills between pairs of edges. This approach handles arbitrary shapes efficiently and naturally supports anti-aliasing in future extensions. 91→

92→ 93→

Edge Structure

94→

95→ Each edge stores its vertical span (top to bottom), its current X position, and its slope for efficient scanline traversal. The dire (direction) field tracks whether the edge runs left-to-right or right-to-left, which is crucial for the winding rule used in complex path rendering. 96→

97→ 98→ 
class Edge {
    99→public:
   100→    int top, bottom;
   101→    float m, x;
   102→    int dire;
   103→    float left_x;
   104→
   105→    Edge(GPoint p0, GPoint p1, GBitmap fDevice, int dir) {
   106→       if (p0.y > p1.y) {
   107→            std::swap(p0, p1);
   108→        }
   109→        top = GRoundToInt(p0.y);
   110→        bottom = GRoundToInt(p1.y);
   111→        left_x = p0.x;
   112→        m = calculateSlope(p0, p1);
   113→
   114→        float b = calculateB(p0, p1);
   115→        x = b;
   116→
   117→        dire = dir;
   118→    }
   119→
   120→    float eval(int y){
   121→        return m * ((float)y + 0.5f) + x;
   122→    }
   123→
   124→private:
   125→    float calculateSlope(GPoint p0, GPoint p1) {
   126→        return (p1.x - p0.x) / (p1.y - p0.y);
   127→    }
   128→
   129→    float calculateB(GPoint p0, GPoint p1) {
   130→        return p0.x - (m * p0.y);
   131→    }
   132→};
133→ 134→

Scanline Filling

135→

136→ The eval() method is the heart of edge rasterization. For any given Y coordinate, it calculates the corresponding X position by evaluating m * (y + 0.5) + b. The + 0.5 samples at the pixel center, which is essential for proper geometric accuracy. 137→

138→

139→ During rendering, edges are sorted by Y position, then processed scanline by scanline. As each row is rendered, the algorithm finds pairs of edge intersections and fills the pixels between them. This approach works for any convex polygon and forms the foundation for more complex path rendering. 140→

Rectangle Rendering

146→

147→ Rectangles are the simplest renderable shape, but they demonstrate the core rendering pipeline. A rectangle is defined by four corner points, which are converted into four edges, then passed through the same scanline algorithm used for all shapes. 148→

149→

150→ The drawRect() function converts a GRect into four GPoint vertices, then delegates to drawConvexPolygon(). The Memory and Register File are typically represented as windows displaying the relevant contents in modern CPU simulators. ## HTML Template Tags and DocumentFragment

The `<template>` element contains a DocumentFragment in their HTMLTemplateElement.content property. The Node.childNodes property of the `<template>` element is always empty, and you can only access said nested content via the special content property.

## Performance Considerations

An important finding from recent documentation: The performance benefit of DocumentFragment is often overstated. In fact, in some engines, using a DocumentFragment is slower than appending to the document in a loop, and the difference between these examples is so marginal that it's better to optimize for readability than performance.

However, DocumentFragment is not connected to the main Document (which is the document tree the browser uses), and modifications to the DocumentFragment does not cause reflow or affect anything in the main document. This can still provide benefits in specific scenarios where you're building complex DOM structures before insertion.

## Key Use Cases

HTML template tag is used to store reusable HTML code fragments that are not rendered when the page loads, and its content remains hidden on the client side and can be activated, cloned, and inserted into the document using JavaScript.

## Overview

CSS Custom Properties have revolutionized the way we write and manage styles, bringing flexibility, reusability, and dynamic theming to modern web design without the need for preprocessors.

## Fundamentals

Custom properties are entities defined by CSS authors that represent specific values to be reused throughout a document, set using the @property at-rule or by custom property syntax (e.g., --primary-color: blue;). Custom properties are accessed using the CSS var() function (e.g., color: var(--primary-color);).

Custom properties are inheritable by default, treating them as "theme values that flow down" that components read, giving you local theming without rewriting every selector.

## Design System Integration

CSS custom properties and Sass variables can be combined to create a powerful theming system that allows overriding system default values. Sass variables act as compile-time constants perfect for immutable brand guidelines, while CSS custom properties serve as runtime-adjustable variables, enabling live theming, CMS overrides, and user-facing customization.

## Responsive and Dynamic Applications

Custom properties are not only useful for theming but can also enhance responsive designs by changing values based on screen size to ensure applications look great on all devices.

## Color-Based Visual Representation in CPU Pipeline Diagrams

In educational illustrations of CPU pipelines, different colored instructions are used to represent stages in the pipeline. For example, a processor cannot decode a purple instruction if decoding depends on results from a green instruction, so the green instruction proceeds to Execute and Write-back stages as scheduled while the purple instruction is stalled at the Fetch stage.

The visual design patterns use blue ovals to represent "bubbles" in the pipeline - idle cycles in the Decode, Execute, and Write-back circuitry. This color-coding helps students visualize how data hazards create gaps in instruction flow.

## Common Pipeline Stage Structure

Each stage handles a specific part of the instruction, such as fetching, decoding, executing, memory access, and writing results. The execution sequence in a pipelined processor can be visualized using space-time diagrams, which commonly use different colors or shading to distinguish between different instructions and their progress through pipeline stages.

## Assembly Line Analogy

An assembly line is a common analogy used in educational contexts, where a pipeline assigns a component to each worker, and as each item moves down the assembly line, each worker performs the same task repeatedly on a succession of items.

These visual patterns with color-coded stages are fundamental to helping students understand how modern CPUs execute multiple instructions concurrently and how pipeline hazards can impact performance.
